strengths: The paper targets a practically important problem: reconstructing animatable 3D head avatars rapidly from heterogeneous, variable-size observations. The unified treatment of single images, monocular sequences, and multi-view captures is appealing. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/3a3e8657d2a247f48bc218086f04e425/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
FastAvatar combines alternating frame/global attention, pose and expression conditioning, Gaussian pruning, and multi-frame supervision into a coherent feed-forward system.

The reported reconstruction results are promising: FastAvatar substantially outperforms the evaluated baselines across PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and identity metrics, while remaining much faster than optimization-based methods.
The experiments cover input counts from 1 to 16, include component ablations, tracking-noise robustness, qualitative cross-dataset examples, long sequences, and wide-viewpoint tests.

The paper includes useful implementation information, failure cases, computational requirements, and an explicit discussion of limitations involving FLAME, eye gaze, wrinkles, and structures outside the FLAME topology.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol is insufficiently specified for validating the headline results. The paper does not clearly report the train/validation/test subject split, number of test identities or frames, sampling protocol, or uncertainty across subjects. Since both training and much of the evaluation use NeRSemble, the claim of performance on unseen subjects cannot be verified and potential identity leakage cannot be ruled out.

The central claim of incremental reconstruction is overstated. Most experiments perform variable-length batch inference by rerunning global attention and concatenating newly predicted Gaussians; this is not inherently an incremental update. Runtime grows from 1.33 seconds for one view to 26.06 seconds for 16 views, Gaussian count grows with input size, and quality nearly saturates after four views. The streaming variant appears only in the appendix, is technically underspecified, and has no quantitative quality, memory, or latency evaluation.

The arbitrary-length claim conflicts with the stated 1–16-frame GPU limit. The FramePack-style extension is supported primarily by a small qualitative example and a plot whose sample size is unspecified. Its global attention still operates on concatenated tokens, so the claim of tractable processing of arbitrarily many frames needs a rigorous complexity analysis and memory/runtime measurements.

Baseline comparisons are not sufficiently controlled. LAM* is an author-created modification rather than an established multi-view method, while optimization-based baselines are given only coarse modeling times of greater than 100 seconds without convergence budgets or tuning details. Avat3r is compared only through images copied from its paper under potentially different conditions, with no quantitative comparison. Other relevant few-shot/generalizable avatar methods appear only in limited qualitative examples.

Important technical details are ambiguous. Equation 3 describes Gaussian fusion as simple concatenation; the exact registration, duplicate handling, canonical anchoring, primitive initialization, and streaming-state update are not adequately formalized. Landmark predictions are not defined, and the sliced-fusion objective is not presented as a distinct loss despite being ablated as one.

Several objective and metric definitions are inconsistent. The written SSIM term is added to a minimized loss without stating that it denotes an SSIM loss rather than similarity. Identity is described as ArcFace similarity but reported with a downward arrow. These ambiguities make the implementation and numerical interpretation difficult to verify.

The ablations do not isolate all claimed innovations, such as the expression/head-pose encodings, positional prompts, LAM initialization, or the FramePack extension. Some components also offer little or inconsistent improvement in the one-view setting. No statistical testing or multi-seed results are provided.

Reproducibility is limited: the abstract says code and models are available but provides no link, while the appendix says they will be released only after acceptance. Training requires eight H100 GPUs for 14 days, increasing the importance of releasing code, preprocessing, splits, checkpoints, and exact baseline configurations.

The ethics discussion understates misuse risk. A seconds-level system claiming reconstruction from a single image does lower the barrier to unauthorized identity reconstruction, contrary to the paper's assertion that it does not. Concrete safeguards, consent assumptions, provenance mechanisms, and discussion of impersonation risks are needed.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: reconstructing animatable 3D head avatars from variable numbers and types of observations using one feed-forward model.

The proposed combination of alternating global/frame attention, pose and expression conditioning, fusion-oriented losses, and Gaussian pruning is technically plausible. The ability to trade reconstruction quality against input count is potentially useful.

FastAvatar reports strong numerical results relative to the evaluated baselines, particularly for 4–16 views, and includes component ablations, efficiency measurements, cross-dataset examples, qualitative failure cases, and a FLAME-tracking robustness test.
The presentation is generally understandable, and the visual results suggest that the method can produce attractive avatars under favorable conditions.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol is insufficiently specified to validate the central results. The paper does not clearly report subject-level training/validation/test splits, test-set sizes, numbers of evaluated identities or frames, sampling procedures, or uncertainty. Because both training and major evaluation use NeRSemble, the absence of an explicit leakage-free identity split is a serious concern.

The claimed incremental reconstruction contribution is overstated. The main method concatenates per-frame Gaussian sets and appears to recompute outputs from a larger input subset; this is not inherently an incremental update algorithm. The streaming and FramePack variants appear only later, are incompletely specified, and receive essentially qualitative rather than systematic quantitative evaluation of quality, memory, latency, order sensitivity, or accumulated drift.

Baseline comparisons are not sufficiently convincing. LAM is modified with an ad hoc fusion procedure that predictably degrades as more independently generated avatars are combined, while Avat3r is compared only through borrowed qualitative examples because its implementation is unavailable. Several relevant generalizable/few-shot avatar methods appear only in isolated appendix examples, and there is no controlled quantitative comparison against the strongest multi-view feed-forward competitor.

Key implementation and reproducibility details are missing, including the exact test protocol, Gaussian initialization and anchoring, dimensions of all predicted attributes, fusion mechanics beyond concatenation, sliced-frame sampling settings, inference-time pruning procedure, and complete FramePack/streaming algorithm. Code is promised only after acceptance, while training reportedly requires 8 H100 GPUs for 14 days.

The ablations do not consistently support all claims. For one view, removing sliced fusion improves several metrics, and the full method is tied with or worse than some variants. There is no ablation separating expression, head-pose, and camera encodings, no comparison against simpler set aggregation, and no evidence that landmark tracking is preferable to other geometric supervision.

Several experimental statements raise credibility or clarity issues: the manuscript refers to a “48GB Nvidia RTX 4090,” although a standard RTX 4090 has 24GB; Table 1 and Table 2 report different full-model values without explaining their protocols; identity is described as similarity but marked lower-is-better; and the reported modeling time reaches 26.06 seconds despite repeated “within seconds” framing.

Generalization evidence is narrow and mostly qualitative. Training uses a single controlled multi-camera dataset, while real-world robustness, tracking failures, backgrounds, occlusions, accessories, lighting changes, camera calibration errors, and demographic variation are not evaluated systematically.

The ethical discussion is inadequate for identity reconstruction. The assertion that the method does not lower misuse barriers conflicts with its advertised single-image, seconds-scale reconstruction capability. Consent, impersonation, biometric privacy, demographic performance, safeguards, and release risks are not substantively analyzed. strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: reconstructing animatable 3D head avatars from variable-length inputs using one feed-forward model. The ability to exploit additional observations is useful and differentiates the system from fixed-input methods.
The proposed system combines alternating global/frame attention, pose and expression conditioning, sliced fusion supervision, landmark tracking, and Gaussian pruning into a coherent design.
Reported results are promising: FastAvatar substantially outperforms the evaluated baselines across 1, 4, 8, and 16 input views while retaining relatively fast reconstruction and rendering.

The ablations cover the principal components and show that global attention and Gaussian fusion are especially important. The evaluation also includes several input regimes, qualitative cross-dataset examples, failure cases, and robustness to FLAME-tracking noise.

The appendix provides useful architecture and optimization details, and the limitations of FLAME/LBS-based animation are acknowledged. weaknesses: The experimental protocol is insufficiently specified. The paper does not clearly report the train/validation/test identity split, number of test subjects or frames, uncertainty across subjects, or whether all main-table evaluations involve strictly unseen identities. This makes the headline quantitative gains difficult to assess reliably.

Baseline coverage and fairness are limited. The main quantitative table omits strong feed-forward competitors such as Avat3r, GPAvatar, HeadGap, and SynShot. LAM* is an author-modified multi-view extension for which performance degrades as views are added, while optimization-based methods are evaluated in unusually sparse regimes; these comparisons do not fully establish superiority over the strongest applicable systems.

The central claim of incremental reconstruction is overstated. Most experiments rerun the model with larger input sets and concatenate more per-frame Gaussians rather than demonstrating an efficient persistent update. Gaussian count, reconstruction time, and rendering cost grow sharply with the number of views, reaching 138.9K Gaussians, 26.06 seconds, and 17.65 FPS at 16 views.

The streaming and long-sequence extensions are described only briefly and supported mainly by qualitative examples. There are no quantitative accuracy, memory, latency, or scaling comparisons against uniform sampling, recurrent updates, or other long-context strategies. Moreover, compressed-frame token count remains linear in sequence length and global self-attention is quadratic in token count, so the claim of sublinear cost is not justified as written.

Generalization evidence remains weak because training uses the controlled NeRSemble dataset, while real-world, cross-dataset, wide-viewpoint, and Avat3r comparisons are predominantly qualitative and sometimes use results copied from other papers rather than a common executable protocol.

Reproducibility is only moderate: training requires 8 H100 GPUs for 14 days, important implementation details remain underspecified, and the manuscript says code will be released only after acceptance despite an incomplete code-availability statement in the abstract.

The ethics discussion understates misuse risk. A fast system capable of reconstructing an identity from a single image can lower barriers to non-consensual avatar creation and impersonation; consent safeguards, provenance, detection, and demographic performance disparities are not meaningfully evaluated.
